title: Christ Is Risen: The Resurrection of the Dead
summary: Paul reminds the Corinthians of the gospel he received and passed on: Christ died for our sins, was buried, was raised on the third day, and appeared to many witnesses, Paul last of all. Against some who denied any resurrection of the dead, he argues that if the dead are not raised, Christ is not raised and faith is futile; but Christ has been raised as the firstfruits of all who belong to him. He then explains the resurrection body, sown perishable and raised imperishable, and ends with a song of victory over death.
story: This is the climax of the letter and one of the most important chapters in the Bible. Paul has saved it for last because the resurrection answers many of the Corinthians' problems: their contempt for the body (chapter 6), their overconfidence that they had already arrived spiritually (4:8), and their preference for impressive wisdom over the message of the cross. Everything in the letter has assumed a future: the Day of the Lord (1:8), the judgment of works (3:13), the saints judging the world (6:2), the Lord's coming (11:26), and seeing face to face (13:12). Now Paul sets out the ground of that hope. The chapter looks back to Genesis (Adam, the dust, a living being) and forward to the end, when death itself is destroyed.
historical:
Verses 3 to 7 preserve a formula Paul says he received and passed on, using the technical terms for transmitting tradition. It uses the Aramaic name Cephas for Peter, is carefully structured in parallel clauses, and lists witnesses by name. Paul says he preached it when he founded the church around AD 50, and many scholars, including many who do not share Christian faith, date his receipt of it to within a few years of the crucifixion (around AD 30 or 33), perhaps during his visit to Jerusalem to see Cephas and James three years after his conversion (Galatians 1:18-19). It is among the earliest Christian testimony to the resurrection that survives.

The witnesses include Cephas, the Twelve, more than five hundred at once, “most of whom are still living” (verse 6), which invited readers to check, James (the brother of Jesus, who had not believed during Jesus's ministry according to John 7:5), all the apostles, and finally Paul. The women who found the empty tomb in the Gospel accounts are not listed; women's testimony carried little weight in public claims at the time, which may explain their absence from a formal list.
cultural:
Many Greeks believed in the survival of the soul after death, but bodily resurrection seemed absurd or undesirable to them. Some philosophical traditions, influenced by Plato, saw the body as a prison or a lesser shell the soul would be glad to leave. When Paul preached the resurrection in Athens, some listeners mocked (Acts 17:32). The Corinthians who said “there is no resurrection of the dead” (verse 12) probably did not deny life after death altogether; they denied that the body would be raised, perhaps thinking of salvation as the soul's escape. Jews, by contrast, commonly (though not universally) hoped for a bodily resurrection at the end of the age (compare Daniel 12:2).

Paul quotes a well-known line, “Bad company corrupts good character” (verse 33), which comes from the Greek comic playwright Menander and had become a proverb. The “firstfruits” (verse 20) were the first sheaf of the harvest, offered to God as a pledge that the rest of the crop would follow (Leviticus 23:10-11). Wild beasts in Ephesus (verse 32) are probably a vivid image of dangerous opponents rather than a literal arena fight, since a Roman citizen was rarely condemned to the beasts.
literary: The chapter is a carefully built argument in four stages. Verses 1 to 11 establish common ground: the gospel both Paul and the Corinthians accept. Verses 12 to 34 reason from that ground with a chain of if-then statements (if the dead are not raised, then Christ is not raised, then preaching is useless, then faith is futile) before turning with “But Christ has indeed been raised” (verse 20) to the order of the end. Verses 35 to 49 answer the question “With what kind of body?” through analogies of seeds, kinds of flesh, and heavenly bodies, and a contrast of the two Adams. Verses 50 to 58 rise into a hymn, quoting Isaiah 25:8 and Hosea 13:14, and end with a practical exhortation. Paul quotes Scripture throughout, including Psalm 8:6 and Psalm 110:1 (verses 25 to 27), Isaiah 22:13 (verse 32), and Genesis 2:7 (verse 45).

outline.t: The gospel received: Christ died, was buried, was raised, appeared
If Christ has not been raised
Christ the firstfruits and the order of the end
Why risk anything if the dead are not raised?
The resurrection body: seed, glory, and the two Adams
The mystery: death swallowed up in victory

doctrines.note: The heart of the gospel is “that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures” (verse 3). His death was not an accident or a martyrdom only; it was for sins, in fulfillment of God's promises. Without his resurrection, believers would still be “in your sins” (verse 17).

The Christian hope is the resurrection of the body, not merely the survival of the soul. What is sown perishable, dishonored, and weak is raised imperishable, glorious, and powerful (verses 42 and 43). The body is transformed, not discarded.
Christ reigns now until every enemy is under his feet, and the last enemy is death (verses 25 and 26). At the end he hands the kingdom to the Father “so that God may be all in all” (verse 28).

Humanity is summed up in two representatives. In Adam all die; in Christ all will be made alive (verse 22). Believers bear the likeness of the earthly man now and will bear the likeness of the heavenly man (verse 49).

words.note: Egeiro, to raise or wake, used nineteen times in the chapter. Paul often uses the perfect tense for Christ (“has been raised”), stressing that he was raised and remains risen. It is the ordinary word for getting up or waking from sleep, fitting Paul's description of the dead as those who have fallen asleep.

Aparche, firstfruits, the first portion of the harvest given to God. Christ is “the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep” (verse 20): his resurrection is the first installment and guarantee of the full harvest of the resurrection of his people. The Jewish Feast of Firstfruits fell during Passover week, near the time of Jesus's resurrection.

Pneumatikos, spiritual. The “spiritual body” of verse 44 does not mean a body made of spirit or an immaterial body. It means a body wholly animated and governed by God's Spirit, just as the natural (psuchikos) body is animated by natural life. The contrast is between powers of life, not between physical and non-physical.

Aphtharsia, imperishability or incorruptibility. The resurrection body cannot decay (verses 42, 50, 53, and 54). Paul uses it to describe the quality of the age to come, which the present body lacks and must be clothed with.

christ: This chapter is the church's clearest early witness to the bodily resurrection of Jesus, a first-order confession of the Christian faith. Christ died for our sins, was buried, was raised on the third day, and appeared to many, all “according to the Scriptures” (verses 3 and 4), meaning the Old Testament Scriptures; Paul names no passage, but interpreters commonly point to texts such as Isaiah 53 and Psalm 16, and perhaps the third-day pattern of Hosea 6:2. Paul stakes everything on it: “if Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile” (verse 17). Christ is the firstfruits of the resurrection harvest, the last Adam who gives life (verse 45), the king who reigns until death is destroyed, and the one through whom God “gives us the victory” (verse 57). His resurrection is the pattern and guarantee of his people's.

hard.q: What does Paul mean by people being “baptized for the dead” (verse 29)?
hard.a:
This is one of the most puzzling verses in the New Testament, and interpreters have proposed dozens of explanations. The most straightforward reading is that some Corinthians were being baptized on behalf of believers (or relatives) who had died unbaptized, and that Paul mentions the practice without approving it, simply to show that it makes no sense if there is no resurrection. Notice that he says “those” who are baptized, not “we.” Others suggest people were baptized for the sake of the dead, that is, becoming Christians in order to be reunited with believing loved ones who had died, or that “the dead” refers to the baptized person's own mortal body. No other New Testament text mentions such a practice, and the mainstream church never adopted it; groups that later practiced vicarious baptism were a small minority.

The verse should not be made the basis of any doctrine or practice, since its meaning is uncertain. Paul's point is clear, however: the Corinthians' own behavior assumes a resurrection they claim to deny, just as Paul's daily risks (verses 30 to 32) would be foolish if death were the end.

questions: Paul says that if Christ has not been raised, Christian faith is futile. Why do you think he was willing to stake everything on one historical claim?
How does the hope of a resurrected body, rather than an escape from the body, change the way you think about your body, aging, illness, and death?
Paul ends a chapter about the future with a command about the present: your labor in the Lord is not in vain. What work are you tempted to think is pointless?
